scenes.tts: How can a cell answer a signal in about a millisecond? Most receptors hand their message to something else, such as a G protein or a kinase. An ion channel hands it to nothing. The signal opens a hole, ions pour through, and the voltage across the membrane changes. One open channel lets about ten million ions cross every second, so which way do they go?
scenes.visual: Membrane and a signal chip; a clock ticks. Beside a normal receptor with G protein and kinase chips below it, an ion channel has an empty 'nothing' box. The gate swings open and ions run through both ways, with question-mark arrows.
scenes.narration: How can a cell answer a signal in about a millisecond? Most receptors hand their message to something else, such as a G protein or a kinase. An ion channel hands it to nothing. The signal opens a hole, ions pour through, and the voltage across the membrane changes. One open channel lets about ten million ions cross every second, so which way do they go?

scenes.tts: Two kinds of protein move ions across a membrane. A pump binds its ions and changes shape to carry them, uphill if it spends A T P. A channel is a pore with a gate, which a transmitter, a voltage, or heat can open. Once it is open, ions run downhill at around ten million a second, while a pump manages a few hundred. So pumps build the gradients slowly, and channels spend them fast.
scenes.visual: A pump (a cup that flips) carries one ion up into a crowd of ions while an ATP badge is spent. A channel gate is opened by three keys in turn, then ions pour downhill from the crowd, many more than the pump moves.

So pumps build the gradients slowly, and channels spend them fast.

scenes.tts: Downhill has two parts: a push from the difference in concentration, and a pull from the voltage across the membrane. Take sodium. A cell keeps it mostly outside, and the inside of a resting neuron sits near minus seventy millivolts. For each ion, there is one voltage at which push and pull balance. That is its equilibrium potential, E, and for sodium it is about plus sixty millivolts.
scenes.visual: The channel patch shrinks left; a push arrow and a pull arrow act on one sodium ion. A voltage scale appears with a marker at minus 70. The marker slides up; the pull arrow shrinks, flips and grows until it equals the push at plus 60, where E is marked.

That is its equilibrium potential, E, and for sodium it is about +60 mV.

scenes.tts: A cell keeps potassium mostly inside. With typical concentrations, E for potassium is about minus ninety millivolts. An open channel drags the voltage toward the E of the one ion it passes. So the direction of flow follows from one subtraction. The driving force is the membrane voltage minus E.
scenes.visual: Potassium crowd moves inside and E for potassium is marked at minus 90. An open potassium channel tugs the marker down toward its E, a sodium channel tugs it up toward its E. Brackets from the marker to each E show a subtraction, then the rule is written.

scenes.tts: At minus seventy millivolts, sodium is one hundred thirty millivolts away from its E. So it rushes in, and the cell depolarises, meaning its voltage becomes less negative. Potassium is only twenty millivolts from its E. So it leaks out gently, and pulls the voltage back down.
scenes.visual: A long sodium bracket reads 130 mV; many sodium ions rush in and the marker rises. A short potassium bracket reads 20 mV; a few potassium ions leak out slowly and the marker eases down.

scenes.tts: Very few ions need to cross to change the voltage. So the concentrations barely shift, and nothing has to be made. The voltage is the message. So keep this rule: the signal opens a hole, and the gradient does the rest.
scenes.visual: A few ions cross and the marker moves a lot while the crowds stay the same. A crossed-out 'new molecules' chip. The gate shuts, then the signal chip lands, the gate opens and the gradient takes the ions down.
